summary: We’re building Lunar Navigator, an interactive tool that helps users choose where and when to land on the Moon. It combines real lunar terrain with Sun and Earth position calculations to show sunlight, shadow, and direct communication windows. Users can compare locations and dates to find suitable conditions for a mission, while Explorer mode makes the science accessible to beginners.
details:
SteppeX’s Lunar Navigator is an interactive web application that helps users explore where and when to land on the Moon. It brings lunar terrain, sunlight, and Earth visibility into one interface, making complex mission conditions easier to understand and compare.

What it does and how it works

Users select a location on a 3D lunar globe and choose a mission date. The application calculates the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to that location, then compares them with the surrounding terrain horizon. This helps identify when nearby terrain blocks sunlight or direct communication with Earth.

An interactive timeline displays sunlight, Earth visibility, and periods when both are available. Users can compare sites and dates, examine extended periods of darkness, and share selected scenarios through a link. Planner mode supports detailed investigation, while Explorer mode explains the science for users without a technical background.

Benefits and intended impact

A location that receives sunlight overall may still experience a long, uninterrupted dark period. Similarly, a site may have sunlight while its view of Earth is blocked. Our project helps users recognize these tradeoffs instead of judging a location using a single percentage.

Our intended impact is to make lunar mission planning more accessible to students, educators, space enthusiasts, and teams exploring early mission concepts. It supports learning and preliminary comparisons; operational landing decisions would require additional engineering analysis and validation.

Tools and development

We built the application using TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Zustand. React Three Fiber powers the interactive 3D environment. Astronomy Engine supports astronomical calculations, alongside a lunar orientation model and calculations of local viewing angles. We used JPL Horizons reference data to check astronomical results and incorporated terrain-based horizon calculations. Vitest and Playwright support testing, and the website is hosted on Vercel.

Creativity and design considerations

Our creative approach connects a visual lunar globe with time-dependent mission conditions. Users can change a location or date and immediately investigate how the conditions change, turning scientific calculations into an experience they can explore.

Our team considered terrain obstruction, lunar orientation, sunlight continuity, direct Earth visibility, calculation speed, and interface clarity. We also considered different levels of scientific knowledge, providing explanations alongside detailed planning information. Throughout development, we focused on helping users understand why a site presents opportunities or difficulties, rather than simply assigning it a score.
